subtitle: Leaders can bring cultural understanding into hiring, onboarding, supervision and development. This course shows how to do so while keeping decisions clear and responsibilities intact.
scope: For leaders, supervisors and team leads across DHS. The employee lifecycle provides practical situations for intercultural learning; the examples do not establish new hiring, personnel or service procedures. You can learn through the full example or reflect privately without entering personal information. This course does not reproduce a CQ or IDI assessment, assign an individual orientation or assign training credit. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA. Learning and reflection are voluntary.
introTranscript: Leadership involves both understanding people and making decisions that affect their opportunities. A familiar expression of initiative, respect or competence may not carry the same meaning for everyone. This course follows practice leader Devon through several employee-lifecycle situations. The aim is to examine relevant meanings, make suitable choices and review what actually happened. Personal insight also matters in its own right; it does not need a workplace result to become worthwhile.

intro.heading: Examine the leadership default you bring
intro.body:
The Cultural Intelligence Center describes four connected capabilities: motivation, knowledge, strategy and action. This course applies those public concepts to original leadership situations. It does not measure your CQ or promise a particular organizational result. The official Intercultural Development Continuum is a separate framework, with five orientations; no course response establishes an individual orientation.

Practice leader Devon associates initiative with quickly offering a personal proposal. Earlier family and community experiences taught Devon that stepping forward was a way to contribute care and take responsibility. In a project discussion, colleague Rowan first checks how an idea would affect other contributors. Devon initially reads the questions as a lack of initiative.

Rowan volunteers a different learned meaning: showing responsibility includes making sure a proposed contribution will not place an avoidable burden on someone else. The questions can therefore express initiative rather than the absence of it. That account changes what Devon can examine; it does not prove that Rowan’s proposal is sound or that all colleagues share the meaning.

Devon can privately understand the connection between taking the lead and showing care. That insight is worthwhile even outside work. At work, it also helps separate an actual contribution from the preferred speed or form of its expression. You can follow the practice learning without disclosing your own background.

flashcards.back: A framework for working effectively across different cultural perspectives; it is not a list of rules for groups.
The interest and motivation to engage across difference.
Understanding relevant cultural differences without turning information into a script for an individual.

Adjusting behavior appropriately to the situation.

items.title: Understand the attraction of your default
items.body: Quick proposals gave Devon a visible way to help. Examining that meaning is more useful than declaring the preference wrong. Devon can retain the value of contribution while noticing that a different sequence may express the same value through concern for others.

items.title: Use information without assigning identity
items.body: Rowan supplied an account of this situation. Devon can take it seriously without making it a rule for people with a similar background. The actual proposal and its effects remain open to examination; personal meaning neither guarantees nor invalidates its quality.

items.title: Keep two legitimate outcomes
items.body: Devon may gain a clearer understanding of a learned value. Devon may also make a better-informed leadership choice. Either can matter. Private insight does not have to generate a recorded work action, and a completed action does not demonstrate someone’s intercultural development.

tabs.label: Reward only the familiar signal
tabs.body: Devon recognizes initiative only when someone offers an immediate personal proposal. The standard may feel clear but overlooks the possibility that careful questions are part of taking responsibility. A preference for speed quietly becomes a judgment about ability.

tabs.label: Replace judgment with a group script
tabs.body: Devon assigns Rowan a cultural category and assumes every future question has the same meaning. This substitutes a positive stereotype for the original negative interpretation. The person’s actual contribution can become less visible behind the new script.

tabs.label: Examine the meaning and contribution
tabs.body: Devon asks what Rowan is trying to protect, then considers the actual proposal. This connects relevant meaning to the work without requiring an identity account. Devon can learn personally while retaining responsibility for the decision.

check.question: What follows from Rowan’s volunteered explanation?
check.correct: Devon has a relevant alternative meaning to examine alongside the actual contribution.
wrong: Every question Rowan asks must now be evidence of initiative.
Devon’s preference proves a particular IDI orientation.
Private reflection has value only after a work metric improves.
check.feedbackCorrect: The explanation can change Devon’s interpretation without becoming a fixed trait, an assessment or a requirement to prove learning through work.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A volunteered meaning is not a guarantee about every future question. A preference cannot establish an individual orientation. Requiring an improved metric would also dismiss legitimate personal insight. Examine the account and contribution without adding those claims.

items.text: Rowan says checking burdens expresses responsibility.
Only immediate proposals show initiative.
How the proposed action would affect contributors.
Devon learned to connect stepping forward with care.
Every person with Rowan’s background must prefer the same sequence.
Whether Devon’s next response helps this discussion.

intro.heading: Examine contribution in a hiring example
intro.body:
In a separate practice hiring exercise, the approved criterion asks for evidence of coordinating a project. Candidate Kai describes a team’s work using “we” and gives limited detail about individual responsibilities. Devon prefers candidates who immediately name their personal achievements and begins to equate that style with stronger leadership.

Kai explains that acknowledging collaborators first is a learned expression of respect. This gives a reason to reconsider the style judgment, but the explanation does not supply the missing evidence of Kai’s own coordination. Both points matter: collective attribution can be meaningful, and the criterion still requires relevant evidence.

Where the actual authorized selection process permits appropriate follow-up, the panel can ask what responsibilities Kai held, what decisions Kai made and how the work was coordinated. Questions and evaluation must follow the approved process and be consistently applied as required. This practice course cannot authorize a new interview method, change a criterion or predict who should be selected.

DHS’s Equity Policy includes recruitment and hiring among the practices reviewed through an equity lens. Leaders should work through the actual HR and selection responsibilities. The useful application here is to examine whether a preferred form is being mistaken for the evidence the real criterion needs.

What should Devon do?
lessons.keyStatement: Seek the evidence the authorized criterion requires rather than reward resemblance to your own style.

items.title: Respect is not evidence of every skill
items.body: Kai’s explanation makes the collective wording understandable. It does not establish project coordination by itself. The panel can respect the meaning while seeking the same job-related evidence that the approved criterion requires, rather than waive the criterion as a gesture of inclusion.

items.title: A follow-up has an authority boundary
items.body: A thoughtful question is not automatically permissible in every selection stage. Devon needs the actual rules for this process. If clarification is not available at that point, the panel must use the authorized route rather than improvise a private advantage for one candidate.

items.title: Examine the process as well as the person
items.body: If the authorized process repeatedly captures presentation confidence while missing the intended skill, that is a process question to review through HR and the applicable equity analysis. It is not a basis for privately rewriting the current selection after seeing a preferred candidate.

tabs.label: Reward resemblance
tabs.body: Devon rates the personal-achievement style as stronger without checking the actual coordination evidence. This can make familiar self-presentation stand in for the approved criterion. The decision may look job-related while its reasoning is partly about resemblance.

tabs.label: Waive the criterion
tabs.body: Devon treats the cultural explanation as sufficient proof and gives Kai a high rating without relevant evidence. This confuses respecting the account with evaluating the skill. It also changes the standard without the authority the actual process requires.

tabs.label: Use authorized evidence
tabs.body: The panel follows its approved process to seek and evaluate coordination evidence. Kai’s wording is not treated as a defect or a qualification by itself. If a process limitation remains, it is identified for the proper review rather than silently repaired through a favored result.

check.question: What is the sound distinction in the practice exercise?
check.correct: Collective attribution can be meaningful while the approved criterion still needs relevant evidence through the authorized process.
wrong: The word we proves a candidate cannot lead.
A cultural explanation automatically satisfies the coordination criterion.
Devon can privately change the current selection standard.
check.feedbackCorrect: Understanding the expression and evaluating the skill are connected tasks with different evidence. The actual selection authority still applies.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Collective wording does not prove inability, and a meaningful explanation does not prove the required skill. Privately changing the standard also exceeds this learning exercise. Keep the criterion and authorized evidence process clear while examining the style assumption.

items.text: The approved criterion concerns project coordination.
Only strong self-promotion demonstrates leadership.
Whether this stage permits a consistent follow-up.
Kai identifies a responsibility held on the project.
Collective attribution must mean weak leadership.
Who can approve a future process change.

intro.heading: Make expectations discussable during onboarding
intro.body:
Practice new employee Samira receives an invitation to ask questions during onboarding. Samira rarely interrupts the group session. Devon assumes the information is clear. Later, Samira volunteers that interrupting a prepared explanation has often meant disregarding the speaker’s effort in prior experience. Samira has questions but has been waiting for a more suitable moment.

Devon can clarify the actual purpose of the invitation: in this session, questions help the team notice what needs explanation. Devon can also identify an appropriate later route within the team’s real responsibilities. Samira need not adopt a particular interrupting style to demonstrate engagement, and the leader should not guarantee a private channel that nobody can support.

A suitable plan might include clearly marked question points and a known contact for the unresolved information. That is an original practice choice, not a new DHS onboarding requirement or a substitute for access and accommodation responsibilities. Devon should check what is actually feasible and authorized.

The important shift is in meaning as well as logistics. A practice framed as participation may initially be read as disrespect. Explaining the purpose and providing a suitable choice can help make the invitation interpretable. Whether it helped Samira remains a question to review, not a conclusion drawn from sending the invitation.

Design a suitable way to clarify expectations within actual responsibilities.
Distinguish an available opportunity from evidence that it was usable.
What fits the situation?
lessons.keyStatement: Make the purpose of a practice clear without requiring newcomers to abandon a meaningful value.

items.title: Clarify the purpose without judging the past
items.body: Devon can explain why questions are welcome here while acknowledging that Samira has learned another meaning of interruption. Calling the previous practice backward would undermine the inquiry. The task is to make the present choice understandable, not rank the experiences that shaped it.

items.title: Offer what the team can actually sustain
items.body: A later contact helps only if the person knows the relevant topic and can respond through the actual route. Devon should identify that responsibility before offering it. A reassuring but unsupported promise can leave a new employee with another unclear handoff.

items.title: Review whether the invitation helped
items.body: Samira’s later question or voluntary feedback can inform a narrow review of this onboarding practice. Silence remains ambiguous. The leader should avoid declaring the invitation successful merely because it was sent or making personal cultural disclosure a condition of getting an answer.

tabs.label: Repeat the same invitation
tabs.body: Devon says the team already invites questions and repeats the wording. This preserves the original format but does not address its different meaning for Samira. A leader may mistake an available invitation for a usable opportunity.

tabs.label: Require the preferred style
tabs.body: Devon tells Samira that active staff interrupt confidently. This makes conformity a test of belonging and may obscure the actual information need. It also turns one learned expression of participation into the only acceptable expression.

tabs.label: Clarify and support choice
tabs.body: Devon explains the question points and identifies a feasible later route. Samira can choose how to raise the relevant issue without a biography or a forced performance. The leader still needs to learn whether the arrangement actually addressed the need.

check.question: What does Samira’s account change?
check.correct: Devon can reconsider the meaning of silence and clarify the purpose and feasible routes for questions.
wrong: It proves all new employees from the same background avoid questions.
It proves the onboarding session already worked.
It authorizes Devon to promise any requested communication method.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account gives a specific alternative interpretation and a practical opportunity to clarify. It does not establish a group rule, an outcome or unlimited authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One account cannot establish a group pattern. The existence of a session does not show that information became usable. A relevant communication need also does not give Devon unlimited authority; suitable choices must connect to the actual responsibilities and access routes.

items.text: Samira explains that interruption can signify disregard.
Identify feasible points for questions.
Silence proves complete understanding.
Samira has been waiting for another moment.
Name the actual contact for an unresolved question.
Everyone with a similar background needs the same arrangement.

Declare the original session successful because it occurred.
responses: Engagement should not be reduced to one performance.
This connects the meaning to an actual usable choice.

lessons.transfer: Use the onboarding example or privately examine a meaning you attach to respectful participation. A personal insight can stand alone; any work application follows real responsibilities.

move.control: You can explain the purpose and the actual choices available.
move.failure: An invitation is treated as proof that everyone can use it in the same way.
move.next: Clarify the meaning, identify the feasible route and leave its effect open to review.

lessons.title: Give supervision that explains the reason
lessons.summary: Distinguish a learned meaning of competence from an actual supervisory responsibility.

Feedback should connect to the actual task.

lessons.statement: Make the reason for supervision clear rather than require one familiar expression of competence.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Give supervision that explains the reason
intro.body:
Practice employee Theo prepares a service communication independently and brings it for review at the required stage. Devon is frustrated that Theo did not seek an earlier discussion. Theo explains that in prior learning, competence meant taking ownership and bringing a considered answer instead of repeatedly asking an authority figure to solve the problem. Devon has associated early discussion with responsibility and trust.

The different meanings can be examined without assuming either is a universal cultural rule. The actual work still has required review stages. Devon can distinguish those requirements from an informal preference for earlier conversation and explain when a discussion is useful for this task.

Useful feedback identifies what the communication needs and why. For example, Devon can explain that an unresolved service instruction should be raised through the actual review route before it is shared. That is more informative than calling Theo uncollaborative. Theo can retain ownership while understanding the purpose of coordination.

If Theo raises a protected-class allegation, the exchange has a separate responsibility. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow their assigned agency procedures. They may have assigned investigation responsibilities; this course does not authorize an improvised investigation or delay reporting for a cultural conversation.

Revise a practice feedback exchange to make expectations clear.
Preserve formal duties while using culturally informed communication.
What should Devon do?
lessons.keyStatement: Make the reason for supervision clear rather than require one familiar expression of competence.

items.title: Separate the requirement from the preference
items.body: Devon should accurately state which review stage is required and which earlier conversation is a suggested support. Calling every preferred step mandatory can make the actual standard unclear. Conversely, presenting required review as optional could leave a consequential communication unexamined.

items.title: Explain the work consequence
items.body: Feedback is more useful when Theo can see the reason for coordination: an unresolved instruction could confuse the person who needs to act on it. The explanation connects the response to the task rather than treating a personal style as a defect.

items.title: Respond through the proper duty
items.body: Understanding the meaning of independence can improve an ordinary exchange. It does not replace reporting a protected-class allegation, authorize a finding or suspend an assigned procedure. The leader can use respectful communication while fulfilling the actual responsibility without asking Theo to resolve it privately.

tabs.label: Make a trait judgment
tabs.body: Devon calls Theo uncollaborative because the first approach was independent. This skips the relevant meaning and the actual task. Theo receives a label rather than an explanation of what needs to happen or why.

tabs.label: Remove every review
tabs.body: Devon interprets cultural respect as allowing any work sequence without required review. This makes meaning override actual responsibility. A suitable response can preserve ownership while keeping the real review stage clear.

tabs.label: Explain and coordinate
tabs.body: Devon acknowledges the meaning of competence and explains the task’s actual review needs. Theo remains responsible for the work, while the supervisory contribution becomes understandable. Formal allegations still receive their required response rather than becoming ordinary feedback.

check.question: What is a suitable supervisory response?
check.correct: Explain the actual task and review requirements while examining the different meanings of independence and coordination.
wrong: Label Theo culturally unable to collaborate.
Waive required review whenever an employee explains a personal meaning.
Delay a protected-class allegation until everyone has discussed cultural intentions.
check.feedbackCorrect: Task-specific explanation makes the supervisory purpose clear while cultural inquiry and formal responsibilities remain distinct.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A trait label replaces useful feedback. A meaningful account does not waive required review. Delaying a protected-class allegation also conflicts with the manager’s immediate reporting duty; respectful inquiry and the required response can proceed without substituting one for the other.

items.text: The service instruction still needs its required review.
Theo connects independent preparation with competence.
Immediately report a protected-class allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.
Explain what remains unclear in the instruction.
Devon prefers an earlier informal discussion.
Follow actual assigned investigation procedures.

responses: This retains ownership and makes supervision useful.
Meaning does not remove the requirement.
A workplace exchange is not an individual assessment.

A clear invitation can coexist with approved criteria.

lessons.statement: Make the opportunity understandable without turning a preferred expression of ambition into its gate.

intro.heading: Make development opportunities visible and fair
intro.body:
Practice team member Riley has not asked Devon for a development assignment. Devon assumes Riley is content with current work. Riley later explains a learned expectation: a trusted leader notices a person’s contribution and invites further responsibility. Repeatedly asking for advancement has felt like disregarding the leader’s judgment.

The explanation gives Devon a reason to question the assumption of no interest. It does not establish Riley’s readiness, guarantee an assignment or define what everyone should want. Another colleague may prefer to initiate the conversation or may not seek the same opportunity at all.

A suitable invitation describes the actual opportunity, approved eligibility or selection responsibilities, available support and a way to express interest. Devon should not offer a private guarantee outside the process or make personal cultural disclosure part of demonstrating interest. The same clarity can help others who have not encountered the opportunity.

DHS’s Equity Policy includes workforce development and retention practices in its equity responsibilities. The original learning here is to examine the connection between meaning and access. Whether a transparent invitation, actual support and authorized selection improved opportunity needs appropriate evidence; an increase in invitations alone cannot establish a fair result.

inThisLesson: Identify an unsupported inference about an employee’s interest in development.
Compare ways to invite interest without promising an outcome.
Distinguish an invitation from actual selection, support and opportunity.
Which response fits?
lessons.keyStatement: Make the opportunity understandable without turning a preferred expression of ambition into its gate.

items.title: Do not make the account another assumption
items.body: Riley’s explanation concerns this situation. Devon can reconsider the absence of a request without deciding that Riley definitely wants every advanced assignment. A respectful invitation makes a choice possible, including declining, rather than replacing one unsupported conclusion with another.

items.title: Keep access and selection distinct
items.body: Making an opportunity visible is not the same as deciding who receives it. A leader should accurately explain the approved process and actual supports. A promised result may feel encouraging but can undermine clarity and exceed the person’s authority.

items.title: Look beyond the invitation count
items.body: An invitation can be recorded as an action where records are appropriate. Usable information, feasible participation and selection outcomes are different questions. Missing feedback remains missing; an optimistic account of access should not be built from the offer alone.

tabs.label: Wait for familiar self-promotion
tabs.body: Devon treats a lack of direct requests as a lack of interest. This may overlook a different learned meaning of respect or a practical access barrier. The opportunity becomes easier to find for people who already know the preferred expression.

tabs.label: Privately guarantee the assignment
tabs.body: Devon promises Riley the assignment as a way to correct the earlier assumption. This moves from inquiry to an unauthorized outcome and can disadvantage others. A meaningful explanation does not replace actual selection responsibilities.

tabs.label: Invite through the real process
tabs.body: Devon makes the opportunity and route understandable, asks about interest and preserves the approved criteria. Riley can choose without supplying a personal history. The leader then reviews whether information and support were actually usable rather than claim success from the invitation alone.

check.question: What does Riley’s account support?
check.correct: Reconsidering the assumption about interest and offering a clear invitation through the actual development process.
wrong: Automatically selecting Riley for the assignment.
Treating every employee who stays quiet as having Riley’s meaning.
Declaring the opportunity equitable because an invitation was sent.
check.feedbackCorrect: The explanation can improve inquiry and visibility. Selection, individual interests and actual effects require their own information and authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Automatic selection exceeds what the account establishes and may exceed authority. Extending Riley’s meaning to every quiet employee makes a script. Counting an invitation as an equitable outcome skips whether it was usable and what the actual process produced.

items.text: Ask Riley whether the described opportunity is of interest.
Explain the approved route and relevant support.
An invitation proves an equitable development result.
Leave room for Riley to decline.
Apply the actual selection responsibilities.
No request proves no ambition.

lessons.title: Connect learning to a proportionate leadership review
lessons.summary: Build a coherent review across the employee-lifecycle examples.
lessons.objective: Build a coherent review across the employee-lifecycle examples.
objectives: Build a coherent review across the employee-lifecycle examples.
Distinguish personal insight, changed practice and observed effect.
Choose proportionate evidence and actual responsibilities for a proposed improvement.
takeaways: Connected experiences can reveal a practice worth examining.
Insight, action and effect are different claims.
Improvement needs appropriate authority and evidence.
lessons.statement: Use cultural learning to ask a better leadership question, then review the actual practice without claiming more than the evidence shows.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Connect learning to a proportionate leadership review
intro.body:
Devon’s practice examples reveal several places where a preferred expression could become a gate: personal attribution in hiring, interrupting during onboarding, early discussion in supervision and self-promotion in development. The connection is a question about how expectations are communicated and evaluated. It is not proof that every process has the same barrier or that one cultural explanation accounts for every outcome.

Devon can identify a specific practice to examine through actual responsibilities. For example, the development invitation could be reviewed for whether it explains the opportunity, selection route and support. Any proposed change follows the relevant HR, decision and DHS equity-analysis requirements. The consultant can guide and offer feedback; staff and leaders retain ownership of their work.

Evidence should fit the question, permissions and privacy. An authorized review of the invitation’s clarity may not require collecting personal cultural histories or disaggregating a tiny team. If a wider equity question needs group information, it requires appropriate data, authority, protection and interpretation. Missing or incompatible information cannot establish either success or failure.

Devon can keep three claims distinct: a personally examined value, a practice changed through the proper route and an effect supported by evidence. Private self-understanding is a valid outcome even when no practice changes. A changed practice is real action even before its effect is known. This gives learning room to grow while keeping an honest account of the work.

inThisLesson: Build a coherent review across the employee-lifecycle examples.
Distinguish personal insight, changed practice and observed effect.
Choose proportionate evidence and actual responsibilities for a proposed improvement.
How can the result be described?
lessons.keyStatement: Use cultural learning to ask a better leadership question, then review the actual practice without claiming more than the evidence shows.

items.title: Choose a focused question
items.body: Asking whether the invitation explains the actual process is clearer than asking whether the team is now culturally intelligent. The narrower question identifies a practice that can be examined. It avoids using a course, a person’s style or a single response as an assessment.

items.title: Keep evidence proportionate
items.body: The invitation text and appropriate voluntary feedback may inform a clarity question. They cannot establish long-term retention or a population disparity by themselves. A wider question may require different evidence and protections, rather than simply adding sensitive fields to the current review.

items.title: Make follow-through owned and honest
items.body: The responsible staff or leader should know what can be changed, who has authority and how an unresolved issue returns for review. Consultant support can strengthen the reasoning without taking over the work. An unanswered effect stays unanswered rather than become a reassuring narrative.

tabs.label: Claim transformation from activity
tabs.body: Devon counts course completion and invitations as proof of a culturally intelligent team. These are activities, not an assessment or evidence of every effect. The claim can obscure the actual question the learning helped the leader notice.

tabs.label: Collect every possible personal detail
tabs.body: Devon gathers cultural histories and small-group data without a clear question or proper authority. More information does not automatically mean better evidence. It can create unnecessary exposure and still fail to explain the practice under review.

tabs.label: Review a specific practice honestly
tabs.body: Devon examines the development invitation through the actual process, uses suitable evidence and separates the action from its effect. Private insight also remains legitimate. This makes improvement assessable without turning staff learning into hidden personnel labels.

check.question: Which account is supported before outcome evidence is available?
check.correct: Devon has examined a personal expectation and may have changed an authorized practice; its wider effect remains unknown.
wrong: Every staff member has moved to Adaptation.
Private cultural reflection failed because no process changed.
check.feedbackCorrect: Personal understanding and actual changes can be described without claiming an individual assessment, retention result or mandatory work outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: No course establishes every person’s orientation. Invitations are not retention evidence. Personal reflection can also be worthwhile without a process change. Keep the insight, action and unknown effect distinct instead of forcing them into one success claim.

items.text: Devon recognizes the learned connection between stepping forward and care.
The authorized invitation is revised to explain its actual route.
Whether participation became more usable has not been checked.
Riley’s explanation changes Devon’s interpretation of silence.
The responsible leader reviews the proposed change through the required process.
Retention cannot be inferred from invitation counts alone.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to examine a leadership choice or retain a private cultural insight without making an unsupported claim.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Devon completes the practice review and revises an invitation through its actual approval route. No evidence of a wider effect is available yet.
scenario.prompt: How can the result be described?
options: Claim retention improved because the invitation changed.
Describe the insight and actual change, keeping the effect open.
responses: This activity cannot supply an assessment.
The changed invitation does not establish a retention result.
This makes the completed work clear without filling the evidence gap.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice lifecycle review or retain a private insight about a learned leadership value. A work application is a choice for relevant real responsibilities, not proof that personal learning mattered.

move.control: You can choose a focused question and describe what is actually known.
move.failure: Activity, personal learning and a supported effect are collapsed into one claim.
move.next: Separate insight, authorized action and evidence of effect.

jobAid.subtitle: Examine a leadership expectation, connect relevant meaning to the employee lifecycle and keep the account of improvement accurate.
remember: A culturally informed account can change a question without becoming a group rule or an assessment.
Personal cultural insight is worthwhile without a required work action or recorded disclosure.
Actual hiring, accommodation, reporting and equity-analysis responsibilities remain in place.

sections.heading: Understand the choice
items: Identify the familiar expression you are treating as evidence of initiative, respect or competence.
Separate the observed action, your interpretation and any meaning the person actually supplied.
Use the example or reflect privately; no cultural history or individual assessment is needed.

sections.heading: Apply within the real responsibility
items: For hiring, preserve the approved criterion and authorized evidence process.
For onboarding and supervision, explain the actual purpose and distinguish requirements from preferences.
For development, make the opportunity and approved route clear without promising selection.

Promptly forward an accommodation request to the appropriate decision-maker and tell the employee who decides, following actual agency responsibilities; supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation.

sections.heading: Follow through honestly
items: Use actual required equity analysis for consequential decisions; program support does not replace the formal route.
Managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow assigned procedures.
Choose evidence that fits the question, authority and privacy; do not automatically collect personal histories or small-group data.
Distinguish private insight, an authorized change and evidence of an effect. Leave unknown outcomes unknown.

sources.title: Cultural Intelligence Center: What is cultural intelligence?
sources.note: Public definitions of the framework and four capabilities. Original leadership cases apply these concepts without reproducing an assessment, relying on commercial statistics or promising improved performance.

sources.title: Intercultural Development Inventory: The Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: The distinct official five-orientation continuum. Course responses, employee styles and leadership examples do not establish an individual orientation; program Integration, where the people a process affects help design it, is not an additional official orientation.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Equity responsibilities extend to recruitment, hiring, onboarding, retention and workforce development. The choices in the example do not replace required analysis or authorize personnel criteria or process changes.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1433: ADA reasonable accommodation
sources.note: Actual request routing, designated authority and medical-documentation limits. A leader’s communication flexibility does not replace the accommodation process or create an agency delegation.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Immediate manager and supervisor reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, assigned procedures and non-retaliation remain distinct from ordinary cultural inquiry.
